title: The Still Face
text:
In the 1970s, the developmental psychologist Edward Tronick and his colleagues in Boston filmed young infants, only a few months old, playing face to face with their mothers. The mothers smiled, cooed and responded, and the babies smiled and babbled back in a kind of conversation.

Then the researchers asked the mothers to do something simple but hard: to keep facing the baby while holding their face completely still and expressionless, not responding to anything the baby did.

The babies noticed almost at once. They tried to get the conversation going again, smiling, cooing and reaching toward the mother. When that failed, they grew wary. Many turned away, slumped, lost control of their posture or began to cry. Some kept glancing back, as if checking whether the mother had returned. When the mothers resumed normal play, most babies recovered, though often with some lingering protest.

The still face procedure has since been repeated in many laboratories and cultures. It showed that even very young infants are not passive receivers of care. They actively take part in social exchanges, expect a response, and are thrown off balance when the person they rely on goes emotionally blank.
lesson: Being physically present is not the same as being there. A child, or anyone close to you, reads your face and feels it when you stop responding.
people: Edward Tronick, Heidelise Als, Lauren Adamson, Susan Wise, T. Berry Brazelton
location: Children's Hospital Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA
source: Tronick, E., Als, H., Adamson, L., Wise, S., and Brazelton, T. B. (1978). The infant's response to entrapment between contradictory messages in face-to-face interaction. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry, 17(1), 1-13.
